Eternal Sonship
ee-TUR-nul SUN-ship
noun phrase (Christology / Trinitarian theology)
The doctrine that the second Person of the Trinity is and always has been the Son of God from all eternity — not becoming the Son at the incarnation or at some point in time, but eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father. Grounded in the eternal generation of the Son and the biblical witness to the Son's eternal pre-existence.

📖 Biblical Definition

The doctrine that the second Person of the Trinity is and always has been the Son of God from all eternity — eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father, not becoming the Son at the incarnation, at the resurrection, or at any point in time. The doctrine is grounded in the eternal generation of the Son (the Son eternally begotten of the Father) and the biblical witness to the Son's eternal pre-existence and eternal filial relation to the Father. The biblical foundation: (1) the Son's eternal pre-existence and glory with the Father — the glory which I had with thee before the world was (John 17:5); before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58); the Word who was in the beginning with God and was God (John 1:1-2); (2) the Father sending the Son into the world (which presupposes the Son's existence as Son prior to His being sent) — God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4); God sent his only begotten Son into the world (1 John 4:9); God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (John 3:16); (3) the eternal love of the Father for the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24); (4) the Son as the eternal only begotten (monogenes) of the Father (John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). The doctrine holds that the Son's sonship is not a function of the incarnation (He did not become the Son by being born of Mary) nor of the resurrection (Romans 1:4, the declaration of His sonship with power by the resurrection, reveals rather than constitutes His eternal sonship), but is His eternal personal property — He is eternally the Son in eternal relation to the Father. The doctrine is distinguished from incarnational sonship (the minority view, held by some, that the Son became the Son at the incarnation) and from adoptionism (the heresy that Jesus was a man adopted to divine sonship). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of eternal sonship as the historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional position: the second Person of the Trinity is eternally the Son, eternally begotten of the Father, in eternal filial relation; He did not become the Son but is and ever was the Son; the incarnation is the eternal Son's taking of human nature, not the beginning of His sonship.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that the second Person of the Trinity is eternally the Son of God — not becoming the Son at the incarnation or in time, but eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father; grounded in eternal generation and the Son's eternal pre-existence (John 17:5, 24; 1:1; Galatians 4:4); the historic orthodox and Reformed position.

ETERNAL SONSHIP, n. phr. (Christology / Trinitarian theology) The second Person of the Trinity is and always has been the Son of God from all eternity — eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father, not becoming the Son at the incarnation, resurrection, or any point in time. Grounded in eternal generation and the Son's eternal pre-existence and filial relation. Foundation: the glory the Son had with the Father before the world was (John 17:5); the eternal love of the Father for the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24); the Father sending the Son (presupposing His prior sonship; Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:9; John 3:16); the eternal only begotten (John 1:14, 18). Distinguished from incarnational sonship and adoptionism. The historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional position.

📖 Key Scripture

John 17:5 — "And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was."

John 17:24 — "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world."

Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

1 John 4:9 — "In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Eternal sonship is the historic orthodox and Reformed position; distinguished from incarnational sonship (the minority view that the Son became the Son at the incarnation) and from adoptionism (the heresy that Jesus was a man adopted to divine sonship).

expand to see more

Eternal sonship is the historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional doctrine, held against two positions. Adoptionism (an early heresy, recurring in various forms) holds that Jesus was a man who was adopted to divine sonship at some point (His baptism, His resurrection); this contradicts the biblical revelation of the Son's eternal pre-existence and deity (John 1:1; 17:5) and is a form of denying the true deity of Christ. Incarnational sonship (a minority view held by some orthodox theologians, notably advocated for a time by certain evangelical figures) holds that the second Person of the Trinity became the Son at the incarnation — eternally the Word or the second Person, but becoming the Son only when He took human nature; this view, while not heretical in the way adoptionism is (it affirms the eternal deity and pre-existence of the second Person), is rejected by the historic orthodox and Reformed tradition as failing to account for the biblical witness to the Son's eternal filial relation to the Father (the Father loving the Son before the foundation of the world, John 17:24; the Father sending the Son, which presupposes His prior sonship, Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:9). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of eternal sonship: the second Person of the Trinity is eternally the Son, eternally begotten of the Father, in eternal filial relation; He did not become the Son but is and ever was the Son; the incarnation is the eternal Son's taking of human nature, not the beginning of His sonship. This doctrine guards the eternal relations of the Trinity (the Father eternally Father, the Son eternally Son) and undergirds the gospel's revelation of the Father's eternal love displayed in sending His eternal Son (John 3:16).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The second Person eternally the Son in eternal relation to the Father; grounded in eternal generation and the Son's eternal pre-existence (John 17:5, 24; Galatians 4:4); distinguished from incarnational sonship and adoptionism; the historic orthodox and Reformed position.
